title: How humans evolved
summary: From the first apes that may have walked upright about 7 million years ago to the end of the last Ice Age, this story follows the fossils, footprints, tools and DNA that show how our family tree grew and branched. Many kinds of humans lived at the same time, met and sometimes mixed, until our own species was the only one left.

chapters.title: The first upright apes?
chapters.text: DNA suggests that our line and the line leading to chimpanzees parted somewhere between about 13 and 5 million years ago. The oldest fossil that may belong on our side is Toumaï, a skull found in the Djurab Desert of Chad in 2001 and dated to about 7 million years ago. The hole where its spinal cord left the skull sits further forward than in apes, a hint that it held its head over an upright body. Orrorin from Kenya, about 6 million years old, and Ardipithecus from Ethiopia, 5.6 to 4.4 million years old, also seem to have walked upright on the ground while still climbing trees. Toumaï's brain was slightly smaller than a chimpanzee's.

chapters.title: Lucy's kind walks upright
chapters.text: About 3.66 million years ago, at Laetoli in Tanzania, upright walkers left trails of footprints in wet volcanic ash that soon hardened. Found by Mary Leakey's team in the 1970s, they are the oldest footprints that everyone agrees were made by a creature walking on two legs. They were most likely made by Australopithecus afarensis, the species of Lucy, a skeleton found at Hadar in Ethiopia in 1974 and about 3.2 million years old. Lucy's kind had brains not much bigger than a chimpanzee's and long arms with curved fingers for climbing, but hips and legs built for walking. A second trail at Laetoli, cleaned and studied again in 2019, has a different shape, so two kinds of upright walkers may have shared the area.

chapters.title: The first stone tools
chapters.place: Lomekwi, west shore of Lake Turkana, Kenya
chapters.text: In 2011, on the west shore of Lake Turkana in Kenya, a team led by Sonia Harmand found stone cores, flakes and heavy anvils in layers dated to about 3.3 million years ago. That is about half a million years older than the oldest fossils of our own genus, so the toolmakers may have been Australopithecus or Kenyanthropus, whose fossils come from the same area. Some archaeologists doubt the date, arguing that the tools could have been washed down a slope from younger layers. The oldest tools of the Oldowan kind, sharp flakes struck from pebbles with a hammerstone, come from Nyayanga in western Kenya, about 2.9 million years old. They lay among butchered hippo bones and teeth of Paranthropus, a big-toothed cousin of ours.

chapters.title: The first of our genus, Homo
chapters.text: In 2013 Chalachew Seyoum found half a lower jaw at Ledi-Geraru in Ethiopia, lying in silts dated by volcanic ash to about 2.8 million years ago. Its shape leans towards Homo, making it the oldest known fossil of our genus. Teeth reported from the same area in 2025 show that early Homo and a new, still unnamed kind of Australopithecus lived there side by side between about 2.8 and 2.6 million years ago. Nearby, at Bokol Dora, toolmakers struck sharp-edged Oldowan tools between 2.61 and 2.58 million years ago. Later came Homo habilis, the 'handy man', named from fossils found at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania in 1960.

chapters.title: Homo erectus: a body like ours
chapters.place: Drimolen cave, Cradle of Humankind, South Africa
chapters.text: A small child's skull, rebuilt from more than 150 fragments dug from Drimolen cave near Johannesburg, is the oldest known fossil of Homo erectus, about 2 million years old. The same cave held the skull of Paranthropus robustus, so Homo, Paranthropus and Australopithecus all lived in South Africa at the same time. Homo erectus had long legs and shorter arms, a body like ours made for walking long distances on open ground. By about 1.76 million years ago, toolmakers at Kokiselei in Kenya were shaping the first hand-axes. The Turkana Boy, a nearly complete skeleton from Nariokotome in Kenya, about 1.5 to 1.6 million years old, was already about 1.5 metres tall when he died as a child.

chapters.title: The first humans leave Africa
chapters.text: By about 1.8 million years ago, humans had reached Dmanisi in Georgia, in the hills between the Black Sea and the Caspian. Five skulls and more than 10,000 simple stone tools have been found there, dated by volcanic rock and magnetic signals to between 1.85 and 1.77 million years ago. The Dmanisi people had small brains, 546 to 775 cubic centimetres, and are usually counted as an early form of Homo erectus. One old man had lost all but one tooth years before he died, so others may have helped him to eat. Stone tools from Shangchen in China are even older, about 2.1 million years, so the first journeys out of Africa may have begun earlier still.

chapters.title: Homo erectus reaches Java and China
chapters.text: Homo erectus reached Java by about 1.3 million years ago, and no earlier than 1.5 million. That date for the Sangiran fossil beds comes from tiny volcanic crystals in the layers above, below and among the bones, and it replaced older estimates of up to 1.7 million years. On the way east, hand-axe makers had reached Attirampakkam in southern India by about 1.5 million years ago. In northern China, the 'Peking Man' fossils from Zhoukoudian near Beijing are about 770,000 years old; the original bones were lost in 1941. Homo erectus lived on in Asia for a very long time, perhaps until about 110,000 years ago.

chapters.title: Early Europeans and the Neanderthal line
chapters.text: Humans were in Spain by 1.4 to 1.1 million years ago: part of a face from Sima del Elefante, in the Atapuerca hills, is the oldest human face yet found in western Europe. Nearby at Gran Dolina, Homo antecessor lived about 900,000 to 800,000 years ago. In a deep pit in the same hills, Sima de los Huesos, lie the bones of at least 28 people, about 430,000 years old. Their faces already have Neanderthal features, and DNA from their bones shows they belonged to the Neanderthal line. Further north, the Mauer jaw from Germany, about 609,000 years old, gave its name to Homo heidelbergensis.

chapters.title: Our species appears in Africa
chapters.text: Skulls, jaws and teeth from Jebel Irhoud, an old cave in Morocco, are the oldest known fossils of our own species, Homo sapiens, about 315,000 years old. They were dated using flint tools found with them that had been heated in fires. Their faces look like ours, but their braincases were longer and lower, so the modern head shape came together only gradually. Fossils from Omo Kibish in Ethiopia, at least 233,000 years old, have fully modern skulls. Together the finds suggest that our species took shape across Africa, not in one spot.

chapters.title: Many kinds of humans at once
chapters.place: Rising Star cave, Cradle of Humankind, South Africa
chapters.text: Deep inside the Rising Star cave system near Johannesburg, excavations from 2013 recovered the bones of at least 15 individuals of a new species, Homo naledi. They lived between about 335,000 and 236,000 years ago, yet had a mix of old and new features: shoulders and hips like Australopithecus, hands and feet more like ours. The Kabwe skull from Zambia, about 299,000 years old, belongs to yet another group, often called Homo heidelbergensis. So Africa held at least three kinds of humans at the same time as early Homo sapiens, while Neanderthals, Denisovans and Homo erectus lived in Europe and Asia. The team that found Homo naledi argues that it buried its dead on purpose, but other scientists say the evidence does not show this.

chapters.title: Denisovans: humans found by DNA
chapters.text: In 2010, DNA from a child's tiny finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia revealed a kind of human that nobody had known about: the Denisovans. They were close relatives of the Neanderthals, and one girl from the cave, nicknamed Denny, had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. Denisovan DNA in the cave's layers goes back about 217,000 years. A jaw from a cave high on the Tibetan Plateau, at least 160,000 years old, and a nearly complete skull from Harbin in China, at least 146,000 years old, have been identified as Denisovan from ancient proteins and DNA, at last giving them a face. Denisovans also had children with our species: up to about 5 percent of the DNA of people in New Guinea and nearby islands comes from them.

chapters.title: Small humans on the islands
chapters.text: In 2003, in Liang Bua cave on the island of Flores in Indonesia, scientists found the skeleton of a tiny adult, about 1 metre tall with a brain of about 380 cubic centimetres. The species, Homo floresiensis, lived there between about 100,000 and 60,000 years ago. Jaws, teeth and an arm bone from Mata Menge on the same island show that very small humans were on Flores by about 700,000 years ago. In 2019 another small species, Homo luzonensis, was named from bones and teeth in Callao Cave in the Philippines, found in a layer about 67,000 years old. Whether these island people came from Homo erectus that shrank over time, or from an older and smaller kind of human, is still argued.

chapters.title: Across the sea to Sahul
chapters.place: Madjedbebe rock shelter, Arnhem Land, Australia
chapters.text: Our species spread out of Africa and along southern Asia to Sahul, the single landmass that joined Australia and New Guinea when the sea was low. Even then, reaching it meant crossing stretches of open sea between the islands of Wallacea. At Madjedbebe, a rock shelter in northern Australia, stone tools, grinding stones and ground ochre lie in layers dated to about 65,000 years ago by measuring light-sensitive signals in sand grains. Other researchers argue that this dating is unreliable and that people arrived closer to 50,000 years ago. A 2025 study of mitochondrial DNA from living people supports arrival about 60,000 years ago, although many geneticists favour the later date.

chapters.title: Meeting and mixing with Neanderthals
chapters.text: As our species spread into Europe and western Asia, it met the Neanderthals, who had lived there for hundreds of thousands of years. Bones from a cave at Ranis in Germany, about 45,000 years old, are among the oldest Homo sapiens in Europe, and their DNA carries Neanderthal pieces from a mixing that happened about 45,000 to 49,000 years ago. Genomes of more than 300 ancient and living people show that most of this mixing happened in one long period between about 50,500 and 43,500 years ago. A person from Peștera cu Oase in Romania, who lived 37,000 to 42,000 years ago, had a Neanderthal ancestor only four to six generations back. Today people in Europe and Asia carry about 1 to 3 percent Neanderthal DNA.

chapters.title: The last Neanderthals
chapters.text: Careful radiocarbon dating of 40 sites from Russia to Spain shows that the Neanderthals' way of making stone tools ended across Europe by about 41,000 to 39,000 years ago. They had shared Europe with incoming modern humans for between 2,600 and 5,400 years, and disappeared at different times in different places. At Gorham's Cave in Gibraltar, researchers argued in 2006 that Neanderthals survived until about 28,000 years ago. But when other late sites in southern Spain were re-dated with cleaner methods they turned out at least 10,000 years older, so most researchers now doubt such late survival. The Neanderthals themselves are gone, but pieces of their DNA live on in most people today.

chapters.title: Into the Americas as the ice melts
chapters.place: Blackwater Draw, near Clovis, New Mexico, USA
chapters.text: Most researchers think that during the last Ice Age people from north-east Siberia crossed Beringia, a land bridge exposed by the low sea, into the Americas. When they first arrived is fiercely argued. Human footprints at White Sands in New Mexico are dated to about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago; critics questioned the first radiocarbon dates, but pollen and luminescence dates published in 2023 agreed with them. Monte Verde in Chile, long accepted at about 14,500 years old, was argued in 2026 to be less than 8,000 years old, a claim its excavators reject. By about 13,000 years ago the Clovis people, named after finds at Blackwater Draw in New Mexico, were hunting mammoths across North America, and, as far as the evidence shows, ours was the only kind of human left on Earth.
